effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative primary study reporting thematic findings from 32 semi-structured interviews and ethnographic site visits; no quantitative effect estimates are reported in this article (one contextual personal communication from Haiti Outreach regarding the central plateau is cited on PDF p. 7, not a primary study estimate).
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Across 32 in-depth interviews and water-source site visits with women in Gressier, Haiti, fragmented short-term NGO/aid provision, limited state oversight, and a lack of infrastructure records shifted the burden of water access, fees, and repairs onto households and informal local actors. Households attempting to obtain piped yard connections relied on self-financed, informal neighbour-to-neighbour PVC extensions (paying up to the equivalent of US$100 for parts and labour with little recourse when low pressure rendered pipes non-functional), faced erratic valve management, community-wide water shut-offs for non-payment due to unclear bill responsibility, and failed reconnection even after arrears were paid. Residents also faced arbitrary padlocking and gatekeeping by local pump managers and precarious courtesy access to wells and springs on private property, whereas communities with active grassroots water organizations reported shared maintenance, training, and mutual financial support.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Primary qualitative study (CASP Qualitative Checklist; design ceiling = 2) that directly documents and observes the institutional, property, tariff/disconnection, and informal gatekeeping mechanisms operating on household water access through 32 in-depth interviews, water-source site visits, and source-manager interviews.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 5–6, Methods; PDF pp. 7–10, 14–16, Results & Discussion

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines private property exclusion from neighbour-owned wells and springs (property); hydraulic/elevation and localized project reach limits (service_area); self-financed PVC connection costs up to US$100, monthly bills, and per-gallon repair/treatment charges (fees); arbitrary valve operation and pump padlocking by informal source managers (discretion); household and community-wide shut-offs for non-payment (disconnection) and failure to restore service after payment (reconnection); grassroots community water committees and collective maintenance (participation); and uncoordinated, short-term NGO/aid interventions lacking accessible records or sustained state oversight (institutional_fragmentation).

outcome_flags.comment: Analyzes household access to drinking and domestic water sources (water_access), installation and functionality of piped yard/home connections (formal_connection), adherence to vs failure of scheduled delivery windows and valve operations (service_reliability), multi-day interruptions, padlocked pumps, and community-wide non-payment shut-offs (service_continuity), low pipe pressure and seasonal source depletion limiting household water volumes (service_quantity), perceived potability, sediment/saltwater/flood contamination, and variable chlorination (service_quality), and financial hardship of up to US$100 connection costs, water bills, and per-gallon or treatment fees (affordability). Sanitation is mentioned only as national background context and is not empirically analyzed.
